                                                        Abstract
          A recent line of work studies language generation in the limit, a formal model of language
     learning where an algorithm observes an adversarially generated enumeration of strings from an
     unknown target language K and must eventually generate new, unseen strings from K. In this
     model, Kleinberg and Mullainathan (2024) proved that generation is achievable in surprisingly
     general settings; whenever K belongs to a known countable collection of languages. However,
     their generator, while quite general, suffers from “mode collapse:” it generates from an ever-smaller
     subset of the target. To address this, Kleinberg and Wei (2025a) introduced a stronger notion of
     dense generation, requiring the output to asymptotically cover a positive fraction of the target, and
     showed it remains achievable for all countable collections.
          Both of these works rely on the crucial assumption of perfect data: the adversary can neither in-
     sert strings from outside the target language (i.e., noise) nor omit strings from it (i.e., omissions). In
     practice, training data for language models is notoriously noisy, raising the fundamental question:
         How much contamination (either omissions or insertions) can language generation tolerate?
    Recent works have made partial progress on this question by studying (non-dense) generation with
    either finite amounts of noise (but no omissions) (Raman and Raman, 2025) or omissions (but no
    noise) (Bai et al., 2026). We characterize the contamination tolerance of both types of generation
    by proving the following results:
  ▷ Generation under Contamination: Language generation in the limit is achievable for all countable
    collections if and only if the fraction of contaminated examples converges to zero. When this condition
    fails, we characterize the collections which remain generable.
  ▷ Dense Generation under Contamination: Dense generation is achievable for all countable collections
    if and only if the amount of contamination is finite. For an infinite amount of contamination, we provide
    several characterizations of when dense generation is possible, showing it is strictly less robust than
    standard generation.
    As a byproduct, we also resolve an open question of (Raman and Raman, 2025) on generation with
    membership oracle access under finite contamination.
    Keywords: generation, online learning, learning in the limit, robustness

1. Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) have transformed text generation and are already seeing wide-
ranging applications from information retrieval to theorem-proving e.g., (Nagda et al., 2025). This
progress has sparked a growing body of theoretical work seeking to understand the foundations of
language generation (Hanneke et al., 2018; Kalai and Vempala, 2024; Kleinberg and Wei, 2025a;
Kalai et al., 2025). We continue this line of inquiry and contribute to incorporating more realistic
aspects of language generation in the hope of yielding sharper insights.
    The study of language generation in computer science is not new; it predates LLMs and dates
back to Turing’s imitation game (Turing, 1950) where he proposed language as a probe of cognition.
Most relevant for us is Gold’s model of language identification in the limit, which formulates learn-
ing as an online two-player game between an adversary and a learner. In this game, the adversary
selects a target language K = Lz from a collection L = {L1 , L2 , . . . }, and starts enumerating K
one element at a time. After seeing each element, the learner’s goal is to guess the index z of K. The
learner is said to succeed if it stabilizes to the right guess z after some finite time (no matter what
elements the adversary shows). A line of work, culminating in the works of Angluin (1979, 1980),
completely characterized the collections which are identifiable in the limit. This characterization
showed that identification is largely intractable; even simple collections like regular languages are
not identifiable in the limit.
    This raises a puzzle: on the one hand, LLMs acquire non-trivial generation ability from just
observing examples; on the other hand, the above model of language learning rules out learnability
even for simple collections like regular languages. Kleinberg and Mullainathan (2024) offered an
elegant resolution to this puzzle by observing that the requirement of generation is weaker than
identification: generation only asks to produce new strings from the language, not to identify the
entire language. To formalize this, they introduce a model of language generation in the limit:
Informal Definition 1 (Language Generation in the Limit; see Appendix F) Fix a collection L =
{L1 , L2 , . . . }. First, the adversary fixes a target language K ∈ L and its enumeration.1 Then, at
step n ≥ 1, it reveals xn ; given the history Sn = {x1 , . . . , xn }, the generator G outputs a new
string wn ∈   / Sn , which is its guess for an unseen element of K. G is said to succeed in generating
from L in the limit if for all K ∈ L and all enumerations of K, there exists a time n⋆ such that for
every n ≥ n⋆ , we have wn ∈ K \ Sn .

 In sharp contrast to identification, Kleinberg and Mullainathan (2024) showed that generation is
remarkably feasible: there is a generator that succeeds for every countable collection L , even the
collection of all Turing-enumerable languages. This surprising positive result sparked a line of
work exploring various aspects of language generation, e.g., (Li et al., 2025; Kalavasis et al., 2025;
Charikar and Pabbaraju, 2025); see Section 5.

Language Generation under Contamination. A crucial assumption in Kleinberg and Mul-

work: Is language generation feasible from training data with large amounts of contamination?
    Two works take an initial step for capturing contamination (Raman and Raman, 2025; Bai et al.,
2026). Raman and Raman (2025) allow finitely many invalid examples (but no omissions) and show
generation remains possible for all countable collections; however, if the amount of noisy examples
is unbounded, then their approach fails. Bai et al. (2026) allow arbitrarily many omissions (without
adding any invalid examples) and, again, show generation is possible for all countable collections
provided infinitely many valid elements remain. This restriction of no invalid elements, however, is
inherent to their approach and their generator fails even with two invalid examples (Appendix F.7).3
    In practice, both invalid elements and omissions persist simultaneously, and in infinite quantity.
Understanding language generation with unbounded quantity of contamination is an important con-
ceptual extension that both brings (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024)’s model closer to reality and
motivates new techniques to handle resulting challenges. This raises our main question:

  Question. How much contamination (both in the form of invalid examples and omissions) can
  generation and dense generation tolerate while still being possible for all countable collections?

Our results present a complete answer to the above question; we present the formal statements of
these results in the next section, but first present a quick summary below.

Summary of Results.          We consider different regimes of the amount of contamination in the
input stream, and completely characterize when language generation in the limit is achievable under
contamination across these regimes. First, we show that language generation shows surprising
tolerance: under natural limits on the frequencies of contamination, generation remains possible for
all countable collections even with infinite contamination of both types (Theorem 5). In comparison,
dense generation is less tolerant: it is possible for all countable collections with finite amounts of
noise (and arbitrary omissions) (Theorem 7 and Informal Theorem 8) but becomes impossible for
all countable collections with any infinite contamination, no matter how sparse (Table 1). Apart
from these main results, we also provide a number of finer-grained characterizations. Our result
extends the results of prior works (Raman and Raman, 2025; Bai et al., 2026) in two dimensions:
(1) we analyze much more general forms of contamination, and (2) if the amount of tolerance
is the same as in prior works, then we can achieve dense generation (for any notion of density)
for all countable collections. Interestingly, all our algorithmic results follow from two algorithmic
templates (Appendix A), explained in the technical overview (Section 4). We believe these templates
can also find applications in other settings of generation in the limit.

Organization. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we introduce
the formal model of language generation in the limit, define the contamination regimes we study,
and review the relevant density notions. In Section 3 we state our main theorems characterizing
when (dense and non-dense) generation is achievable under different forms of contamination, and
in Section 4 we give a technical overview of the key algorithmic ideas and proof strategies. Finally,
Section 5 discusses related work, and Section 6 concludes with discussion and open problems.

3. Our Results
Our first result studies generation under contamination.
Theorem 5 (Generation with Contamination) There is a generator that, for any countable lan-
guage collection L , generates in the limit from L under o(1)-noise and arbitrary omissions.
Thus, generation is quite tolerant to contamination: even with infinite contamination, it remains
possible for all countable collections when the noise-fraction tends to 0. This significantly gener-
alizes both Raman and Raman (2025); Bai et al. (2026). It might seem surprising that we impose
no constraint on omissions; this stems from generation’s asymmetric objective: it requires generat-
ing new unseen elements, thus penalizing false positives more than false negatives. Our generator
utilizes a novel idea: it carefully re-orders languages based on the adversary’s actions, contrasting
with existing generators that use static orderings (Section 4). Further, it outputs (elements from)
intersections of certain languages and, hence, is not an index-based generator; we show that this is
necessary (Remark 10 and Example 8). The formal proof is deferred to Appendix B.1. Next, we
show the requirement of o(1)-noise is necessary.

Informal Theorem 6 (Generation with c-contamination; see Theorem 16) Fix any c ∈ (0, 1).
Under c-noise and arbitrary omissions, a countable language collection L is generable in the limit
if and only if L satisfies the condition in Theorem 16 with parameter c.
    Moreover, for each c ∈ (0, 1), there is a finite collection L that violates this condition.

This result reveals the limits of generation’s contamination tolerance. While we omit the technical
details of the condition, we note that all finite collections of size at most 1/c satisfy the condition
with parameter c. This generator also uses the idea of carefully reordering languages. The proof of
this result can be found in Appendix B.2.
Dense Generation with contamination. Next, we turn to dense generation.
Theorem 7 (Dense Generation with Contamination I) Under finite contamination and for any
countable collection L : (i) there is a generator achieving set-based upper density 1; (ii) there is a
generator achieving element-based upper density ρ = 1/2; and (iii) there is a generator achieving
element-based lower density ρ = 1/8.

To understand our (meta) algorithm, it is instructive to first understand the algorithm of Charikar and

Then, it initializes Ot ← Σ∗ and traverses the list Lσ(1) , . . . , Lσ(ℓ) . If Ot ∩ Lσ(j) = ∞ it updates
Ot ← Ot ∩ Lσ(j) , otherwise it proceeds to the next element without changing Ot .
     Of course, this algorithm does not directly work when there is contamination in the sample
stream because, for instance, the consistency check of L ̸⊇ Sn is no longer meaningful. Consider
the case of c-noise; let the enumeration be E = {x1 , x2 , . . . }. The natural counter part is to check
whether E is an c-noisy enumeration of L. This, however, requires having access to the entire
enumeration E, which we have never seen at any iteration n < ∞. One could instead check if the
fraction of elements from {x1 , x2 , . . . , xn } not in L, which we term the empirical noise rate, is at
most c + ε for small fixed ε > 0. There are examples where this fails because this approach can
include “bad” languages L that do not meet the actual requirement that E is a c-noisy enumeration
for L. One could tighten this check by setting ε = 0, but then we run into the issue that the
empirical noise rate for certain bad languages can fluctuate above and below c infinitely often. To
gain some intuition suppose K = {2, 4, 6, . . . } and L = {n : n ∈ N, n mod 4 ̸= 0} ∩ A where
A = ∪ℓ∈N [(2ℓ)!, (2ℓ + 1)!]. Then, the enumeration E = {1, 2, 3, . . . }, is a 1/2-noisy enumeration
for K and 3/4-noisy enumeration of L (so L should be excluded in our check). However, the
empirical noise rate of L fluctuates between 0 and 3/4 infinitely often (and, hence, L would end up
being included in our check infinitely often).
     This is not merely a superficial problem in the above approaches, but rather an inherent prob-
lem in verifying c-noise or o(1)-noise at finite times — which is impossible as they are necessarily
limiting phenomena. Hence, to overcome this we need a new approach that is able to (i) remove
“bad” languages from our “active set” of languages, and (ii) ensure that the target language K al-
ways remains in this set after some finite time. To design our approach, we take inspiration from the
failure of the above approaches, where certain “bad” languages fluctuate between passing our check
and failing our check infinitely often. Our algorithm assigns each language a priority. Initially, the
priority of language Li is simply −i (so the languages in order of priority are L1 , L2 , . . . ), and each
time Li fails our check we penalize the language by decreasing its priority. The key observation
is that even though K might be getting penalized infinitely often, it will, eventually, be part of a
stable prefix. Then, taking intersections of prefixes, as long as these remain infinite ensures that in
the limit, we output subsets of K. Similar properties of the orderings induced by priorities enable
us to get appropriate notions of density.
     Like our previous algorithmic template, this also has quite general applicability: to all notions of
density and also for generation with bounded adversaries. Indeed, this core algorithmic template of
assigning priorities to languages shows up in all of our algorithms beyond the finite contamination
regime, each time, with a slightly different notion of priority. For instance, with M -bounded adver-
saries, we need to check whether the provided enumeration E is indeed M -bounded for a langrage
L; this is again a limiting phenomenon which cannot be checked at any finite time. The situation
for dense generation is even more complicated. Indeed, Kleinberg and Wei (2025a) already demon-
strated that achieving lower density (both element-based set-based) for all countable collections is
very difficult and their algorithms carefully need to balance the trade-off between generating only

assign to each language is a function of both the “loss” term and a “regularization” term, similar to
the regularized ERM. However, the priority-based intersection algorithm diverges from regularized
ERM in the output rule. Instead of outputting a single language with the minimum “risk”, the
priority-based intersection algorithm outputs from the intersection of a carefully chosen collection
of languages with the lowest risks.
4.2. Lower Bounds for Dense and Non-Dense Generation
A common theme in learning theory is that, once we have the “right” algorithm, we can obtain
tight lower bounds by understanding when the algorithm fails. This is also the case with our lower
bounds, which are derived by first understanding the obstructions to generability (with different no-
tions of density and contamination) and then formalizing them using diagonalization arguments. An
interesting property of our lower bounds is that many of them have a finite witness. For instance,
consider dense generation with finite contamination. All our characterizations here have the follow-
ing form: A countable collection L violates the condition if there are two pathological languages
L1 , L2 ∈ L with a certain property. (For example, that L1 ⊆ L2 and µlow (L1 , L2 ) = 0.) This
contrasts existing lower bounds in generation and identification which required infinite witnesses.
For instance, Kleinberg and Wei (2025a) showed that the existence of an infinite perfect tower
characterizes lower set-based density. However, as its name suggests, an infinite perfect tower is
necessarily witnessed by an infinite sub-collection of languages. Similarly, the characterizations
of identification in the limit (Angluin, 1980) and language generation with breath (Kalavasis et al.,
2025; Charikar and Pabbaraju, 2025; Kalavasis et al., 2026) also require infinite witnesses.

5. Further Related Work
5.1. Related Work on Language Identification in the Limit
Starting from Gold (1967) there has been a rich line of work including both linguistics and com-
puter science on the model of language generation in the limit. Of particular relevance to our work
are the line of works on language identification in the limit in settings where the adversary can
include invalid examples in the enumeration (i.e., noise) or omit elements (Mukouchi and Sato,
2003b; Case et al., 1997; Stephan, 1997; Baliga et al., 1992; Fulk and Jain, 1989; Schäfer, 1985).
In particular, Jain (1994) extends Gold’s model to streams with infinitely many inaccuracies, con-
trolling corruption via density (covering finite, vanishing, and constant-rate noise). Mukouchi and
Sato (2003a) use a neighbor-system (metric) model that permits insertions and deletions provided
each corrupted item lies within a fixed distance of some true string. Tantini et al. (2006) analyze the
same metric-based setting and prove identification results under such systematic noise.

5.2. Related Work on Language Generation in the Limit
Next, we discuss works on language generation in the limit. We have already discussed some of
these works in the introduction. We discuss the key related works here, and then defer a detailed
and thorough discussion of other works to Appendix G.

(2024)’s model has been extended along another axis: the enumeration of examples. While Klein-

are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution P supported on K. In this model, they obtain the first
and near-tight sample complexities of identification in the limit, generation in the limit, and related
tasks. Apart form (Bousquet et al., 2021), (Kalavasis et al., 2025)’s model was also described by
Angluin (1988) in the context of language identification. This stochastic model is incomparable to
the worst-case to the bounded displacement model we study here. It is an interesting question to
understand if the stronger results we obtain for dense generation in the bounded-adversary model
can also be obtained in the statistical model.
Noise and Omissions. As already mentioned in Section 1, the two most relevant works are Raman
and Raman (2025) and Bai et al. (2026). Raman and Raman (2025) initiated the study of language
generation with a finite amount of additive noise n⋆ (unknown to the generator), characterizing the
classes that are uniformly generable in this setting. In particular, their results imply that all countable
collections remain generable with finite additive noise. Bai et al. (2026) show that infinite omissions
do not change which collections are uniformly or non-uniformly generable; combined with Charikar
and Pabbaraju (2025), this implies that all countable collections remain non-uniformly generable
with infinite omissions. They also study the finite-additive-noise setting of Raman and Raman
(2025), providing a characterization of non-uniform generation in that regime. The main additional
challenges in our work are: (i) handling an infinite amount of additive noise, where the algorithms
from these prior works fail, and (ii) simultaneously handling both additive noise and omissions.
Breadth and Density. Prior to the density-based definitions of “breadth” proposed by Kleinberg
and Wei (2025a), the parallel works of Kalavasis et al. (2025); Charikar and Pabbaraju (2025);
Kalavasis et al. (2026) introduced more stringent notions, requiring (roughly) that the set of elements
the generator can produce at each timestep eventually becomes a subset of K missing only finitely
many elements. They characterized when such breadth is achievable. Moreover, Kalavasis et al.
(2025) introduced and studied a statistical model and Charikar and Pabbaraju (2025) explored role
of “feedback” and non-uniform generation, with different types of oracles. (Non-uniform generation
studies how quickly the learner can start outputting valid, unseen elements of K.) Separately, Peale
et al. (2025) introduced “representative generation,” where strings are partitioned into groups and
the generator must eventually represent all groups; a relaxation of the breadth notions above.
Concurrent and Independent Work. Independent and concurrent work by Kleinberg and Wei
(2025b) also studies dense language generation with omissions but without noise. Their main result
is a generator with element-based lower density (1−c)/2 under c-omissions (Appendix F), which
is tight. Our works share some qualitative ingredients: both use a generator that infinitely often
outputs a set containing all observed examples and contained in K, and both observe that proper
(index-based) learning fails under omissions. Beyond this, the works diverge: Kleinberg and Wei
(2025b) optimize density under omissions, while we handle both noise and omissions across various
regimes (Appendix A.1) and study a beyond-worst-case model. Their tight density bounds also have
implications for our results, improving Theorem 7 from 1/8 to 1/2. See Appendix F.8 for details.

6. Discussion and Open Problems
In this work, we characterized the contamination tolerance of language generation in the limit (The-
orems 5 and 7 and Informal Theorem 8). We showed that standard generation can tolerate contam-
ination in infinite quantity, only requiring that the fraction of contaminated examples converges to
zero. Dense generation, in contrast, can only tolerate finite amounts of contamination. Thus, the
additional coverage guarantees of dense generation come at a cost in robustness.
    There are several interesting future directions related to noisy generation, and more broadly, the
line of work on generation in the limit. An interesting direction is to fully characterize element-
based generation for all types of contamination model we study. Further, our finite-contamination
algorithm uses only membership oracle access to L , but several of our other algorithms require
more powerful oracles; understanding what can be achieved with simpler oracles remains open.
Finally, beyond restricting the adversary, another way to circumvent our lower bounds may be
to relax the learner’s requirements: how does the landscape of (noisy) generation change if the
generator may output a vanishing fraction of hallucinations? We note that a similar question was
posed by Kleinberg and Wei (2025a) in the context of improving density guarantees.

Hardness of Identification. Since we have introduced a new model that is limiting the power of
the adversary, it is worth understanding how restrictive this change is. Towards that end, we study

Theorem 37 There is a countable collection L for which no algorithm can identify in the limit,
even when restricted to M -bounded enumerations for any M > 1.

Proof Let L = {N} ∪ {N \ {n} : n ∈ N} be the collection consisting of the natural numbers and
all its subsets obtained by deleting a single number. Let A be any algorithm.

are done. Let n1 be the first step when A outputs N. Then at step n1 + 1, we output n1 + 2 instead of
n1 +1 and then continue enumerating the natural numbers in the canonical order. If A never outputs

step n2 + 1, the adversary “fills in” the previously skipped element by outputting n1 + 1, instead of
n2 + 1, and then continues enumerating the natural numbers in the canonical order again. Repeat.

time. On the other hand, if we let σ(n) denote the value of the element the adversary enumerates
at step n, then σ(n) ≤ n + 1. Thus identification in the limit remains impossible in general even
under M -bounded displacement enumerations, for any M > 1.

the same first unseen element, unless it has already been output due to a previous step caused by a
repetition. Note here we crucially used the fact that the infinite set we are picking from is only a
function of the (unique) input enumeration.

F.7. Discussion of Bai et al. (2026)’s Approach

The approach of (Bai et al., 2026) for generation with omissions is fragile to noise. They show
that if a generator for L begins (valid) generation after n⋆ iterations in the noise-free, omission-
free setting (where n⋆ depends on K ∈ L but not on the adversary’s enumeration of K) then the
same generator handles arbitrary omissions. Such a generator for countable collections was given
by (Charikar and Pabbaraju, 2025). However, this approach fails with noise. To see this, consider
the collection L = {K, L1 , L2 , . . .} where

                     K = N,
                     Li = {−1, −2} ∪ {1, 2, . . . , i − 1} ∪ T ,    for each i ∈ N ,
                      T = {. . . , −102, −101, −100} .

Let the target be K = N with enumeration E = (−2, −1, 1, 2, 3, . . .), containing just two noisy
examples. At iteration n ≥ 2, after observing {−1, −2, 1, . . . , n − 2}, the only consistent language
among L1 , . . . , Ln is Ln−1 . The algorithm of (Charikar and Pabbaraju, 2025) therefore generates
from T ⊂ Ln−1 . Since T ∩ K = ∅, it never generates valid elements. This demonstrates that noise-
free generation strategies cannot be directly applied to noisy settings, even with minimal noise.


F.8. Comparison to Kleinberg and Wei (2025b)

Recently, Kleinberg and Wei (2025b) independently and concurrently followed up on their earlier
work (Kleinberg and Wei, 2025a). The follow-up (Kleinberg and Wei, 2025b) explores dense lan-
guage generation under omissions (but without noise). They prove the following results:

R1. Their main result is a generator that, for any countable collection L , given an enumeration
    with c-omissions (see Definition 4 for definition), generates L in the limit with element-based
    lower density at least (1−c)/2 (which is also tight).
R2. A key ingredient in this result is a generator that, for any countable collection L , given enu-
    meration (x1 , x2 , . . . ), infinitely many times t outputs a set Gt with {x1 , x2 , . . . } ⊆ Gt ⊆ K.
R3. Apart from this, they (1) study a notion of partial identification in the limit, providing a charac-
    terization, and (2) observe that index-based or proper learning is too restrictive in the presence
    of omissions.

We also prove R2 above using a very similar algorithm to theirs (Theorem 17), as well as observe
that proper learning is impossible with omission (Example 8). These are the only explicitly shared
results between our works. Adding to R3, we show that proper learning is impossible with noise
(Example 7). (Kleinberg and Wei, 2025b) takes the generator in R2 to further prove R1. We take the
generator in R2 further in a different direction to handle various amounts of noise (see Table 1); and,
given its repeated use, we formalize this as an algorithmic template capturing it which could have
broader use in the study of language generation (Appendix A.1). Apart from this, we also study
the beyond-worst case model and prove stronger dense-generation guarantees under this model
(Appendix D).

Appendix G. Further Related Work on Language Generation
In Section 5, we presented works on language generation in the limit most directly related to our
contributions. Here, we discuss additional works on language generation that provide useful context
but are less central to our results.
Language Generation with Uncountable Collections. As we mentioned in Section 1, (Kleinberg
and Mullainathan, 2024) introduced the model of language generation in the limit. While they and
many subsequent works, including ours, focus on the setting where the collection of languages is
countable, Li et al. (2025) extended the study to uncountable collections of languages. (Li et al.,
2025) introduced two more fine-grained notions of language generation: uniform and non-uniform
generation. Uniform generation requires the number of strings n⋆ the generator needs to see before
starting to generate (see Definition 1) to be independent of the choice of the targe language K. Non-
uniform generation allows n⋆ to depend on K, but requires it to be independent of the enumeration
of K chosen by the adversary. (Note that generation in the limit allows n⋆ to be dependent of both K
and the enumeration of K.) (Li et al., 2025) characterized the collections that are uniformly genera-
ble as well as collections that are non-uniformly generable. The latter characterization, in particular,
demonstrates that all countable collections can be non-uniformly generated although with a differ-
ent algorithm than that of (Kleinberg and Mullainathan, 2024); this result was also concurrently and
independently obtained by Charikar and Pabbaraju (2025). Interestingly, Charikar and Pabbaraju
(2025) showed that this type of generation is impossible if the learner only has membership oracle
access to L . (Li et al., 2025) gave several sufficient conditions for uncountable collections to be
generable in the limit and left a complete characterization as an open problem. En route to obtaining
a complete characterization, they left other open problems, notably checking closedness under finite
unions: if L1 , L2 , . . . , Lk are generable in the limit, then is ∪ki=1 Li also generable in the limit?
(Hanneke et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2026) concurrently and independently resolved this problem by
showing that the statement is false even with k = 2. Their proofs are near-identical and rely on a
diagonalization argument which has also been featured in other works on language generation as
discussed in Section 5.
Further Works on Language Generation. Apart from the aforementioned works on language
generation, there are two other recent papers studying this framework. Charikar and Pabbaraju
(2026) study a notion of Pareto-optimal non-uniform generation, which seeks to obtain algorithms
that achieve the Pareto frontier for non-uniform generation. On a different front, Karbasi et al.
(2025) propose and study a theoretical model of hallucination detection that is inspired by the lan-
guage identification and generation settings. Lastly, Vafa et al. (2024) propose a theoretical model
that measures the proximity between the language represented by an LLM and the language it was
trained on.
